greet.speaker: host

line.zh: 早上好！欢迎光临！请问几位？有预订吗？
line.zht: 早上好！歡迎光臨！請問幾位？有預訂嗎？
line.py: Zǎoshang hǎo! Huānyíng guānglín! Qǐngwèn jǐ wèi? Yǒu yùdìng ma?
line.en: Good morning, welcome! How many of you, and do you have a reservation?

greet.note: You're here with a friend. Dim sum is traditionally a morning meal — 早茶 (zǎochá), "morning tea".

choices.feedback: Both questions answered. Note 两 (liǎng), not 二 (èr), before a measure word like 位.
Good use of 两位 — but she also asked 有预订吗 ("do you have a reservation?"). Answer both: 没有预订.
Hungry already! First she needs 几位 (how many people) and whether you have a 预订 (reservation).

wait.speaker: host

line.zh: 现在要等十分钟左右，可以吗？
line.zht: 現在要等十分鐘左右，可以嗎？
line.py: Xiànzài yào děng shí fēnzhōng zuǒyòu, kěyǐ ma?
line.en: There's about a ten-minute wait right now. Is that okay?

wait.note: Busy teahouses often hand out a numbered ticket (号码牌, hàomǎ pái) while you wait. 左右 (zuǒyòu) after a number means "about".

choices.feedback: Polite and easy. 等一下 (děng yíxià) = "wait a bit".
没问题 (méi wèntí), "no problem", is one of the handiest phrases there is.

text.py: Tài màn le! Wǒ bù děng!

choices.feedback: That's rude — and you'd miss out on dim sum! Ten minutes is normal on a busy morning.

seated.speaker: narrator

line.zh: 十分钟后，你们坐下了。桌上有一张点心单。
line.zht: 十分鐘後，你們坐下了。桌上有一張點心單。
line.py: Shí fēnzhōng hòu, nǐmen zuò xià le. Zhuō shang yǒu yì zhāng diǎnxīn dān.
line.en: Ten minutes later you're seated. There's a dim sum order sheet on the table.

seated.note: 张 (zhāng) is the measure word for flat things like paper, tables, and tickets.

tea.speaker: server

line.zh: 你们好！喝什么茶？我们有普洱、铁观音和菊花茶。
line.zht: 你們好！喝什麼茶？我們有普洱、鐵觀音和菊花茶。
line.py: Nǐmen hǎo! Hē shénme chá? Wǒmen yǒu pǔ'ěr, tiěguānyīn hé júhuā chá.
line.en: Hi! What tea would you like? We have pu'er, Tieguanyin, and chrysanthemum.

tea.note: Tea comes first — 饮茶 (yǐnchá) literally means "drink tea". Most teahouses add a per-person tea charge (茶位费, cháwèi fèi).

choices.feedback: 来 (lái), "bring", is the casual way to order. 壶 (hú) is the measure word for a pot.
A fragrant oolong named after Guanyin, the goddess of mercy — great with richer dishes.
Light and floral. It's considered "cooling" (清热) — a nice balance for fried dim sum.

text.py: Wǒ bú yào chá, gěi wǒ kělè.
text.en: No tea — give me a cola.

choices.feedback: At a teahouse, tea is the whole point — and the tea charge is usually added anyway. Pick a tea!

tea-pour.speaker: narrator

line.zh: 茶来了。你先给朋友倒茶。朋友用两根手指轻轻敲了敲桌子。
line.zht: 茶來了。你先給朋友倒茶。朋友用兩根手指輕輕敲了敲桌子。
line.py: Chá lái le. Nǐ xiān gěi péngyou dào chá. Péngyou yòng liǎng gēn shǒuzhǐ qīngqīng qiāo le qiāo zhuōzi.
line.en: The tea arrives. You pour for your friend first. Your friend lightly taps the table with two fingers.

tea-pour.note: Pour for others before yourself — it's basic tea etiquette.

choices.feedback: Right! Tapping two fingers (叩指礼, kòuzhǐ lǐ) silently thanks whoever pours your tea.
choices.note: Legend says an emperor travelling in disguise poured tea for his servants; unable to kowtow in public, they tapped bent fingers on the table instead.

choices.feedback: Close — it's tea-related, but it's a silent “thank you” for pouring. (There's a different signal for more water. You'll see!)
Not at all — it's a polite gesture, not an impatient one.

cart.speaker: cart

line.zh: 虾饺、烧卖，刚出笼的！要不要？
line.zht: 蝦餃、燒賣，剛出籠的！要不要？
line.py: Xiājiǎo, shāomài, gāng chū lóng de! Yào bu yào?
line.en: Shrimp dumplings, siu mai — fresh out of the steamer! Want some?

cart.note: Push carts (点心车, diǎnxīn chē) roam the room. Wave the auntie over and point. 要不要 (yào bu yào) is a yes/no question: "want or not?"

text.en: One basket of shrimp dumplings, please!

choices.feedback: 笼 (lóng), "steamer basket", is the measure word for dim sum.
样 (yàng) means "kind" — 两样都要 is "we want both kinds".
She'll understand — but dim sum comes by the basket. Say 一笼 (yì lóng), not 一个. You get a whole basket!
不用了 (bú yòng le) is the polite way to decline. You can still order from the sheet.

stamp.speaker: cart

line.py: Hǎo, wǒ gěi nǐmen gài ge zhāng.

stamp.note: Cart dishes are recorded with a stamp (盖章, gài zhāng) on the card at your table — the bill is added up from it at the end.

order-sheet.speaker: server

line.zh: 还想加点什么？可以在点心单上打勾。
line.zht: 還想加點什麼？可以在點心單上打勾。
line.py: Hái xiǎng jiā diǎn shénme? Kěyǐ zài diǎnxīn dān shang dǎ gōu.
line.en: Anything else? You can tick what you want on the order sheet.

order-sheet.note: 打勾 (dǎ gōu) means "to make a check mark".

line.py: Hǎo de, nǐmen diǎn le {order}. Duì ma?
line.en: Okay, you've got: {order}. Is that right?

choices.feedback: Order confirmed. Time to eat!
Sure — here's the sheet again.

line.zh: 吃了一会儿，茶壶空了。怎么加水？
line.zht: 吃了一會兒，茶壺空了。怎麼加水？
line.py: Chī le yíhuìr, cháhú kōng le. Zěnme jiā shuǐ?
line.en: After a while, the teapot is empty. How do you get more hot water?

text.py: Bǎ húgài dǎkāi, fàng zài yì biān.
text.en: Lift the lid and set it to one side.

choices.feedback: The classic silent signal — staff will top up your pot without a word.

text.en: Excuse me, could we have more water, please?

choices.feedback: Also perfect. 麻烦 (máfan), "sorry to trouble you", makes any request polite.
Please don't! Just leave the lid open, or ask for 加水 (jiā shuǐ).

line.py: Lái le, gěi nǐmen jiā shuǐ.

line.zh: 吃饱了。你的朋友说：“今天我请客！”
line.zht: 吃飽了。你的朋友說：「今天我請客！」
line.py: Chī bǎo le. Nǐ de péngyou shuō: “Jīntiān wǒ qǐngkè!”
line.en: You're full. Your friend says: “It's my treat today!”

text.py: Bù xíng bù xíng, zhè cì wǒ lái!
text.en: No, no — this time it's on me!

choices.feedback: Politely "fighting" over the bill (抢着买单) is classic Chinese dining etiquette. You insisted, so you pay.
choices.note: Next time your friend will insist on treating you — that's how it evens out.

choices.feedback: AA制 (AA zhì), going Dutch, is common among young friends and coworkers. You pay now; your friend sends their half by phone.
Fine between close friends, but it's polite to offer at least once. (Your friend then "forgets" their wallet — you're paying!)

line.zh: 你想结账。怎么叫服务员？
line.zht: 你想結賬。怎麼叫服務員？
line.py: Nǐ xiǎng jiézhàng. Zěnme jiào fúwùyuán?
line.en: You want to pay. How do you call the server?

choices.feedback: 埋单 (máidān) is the Cantonese-style way to write 买单 — perfect for a Cantonese teahouse.

text.en: Excuse me, we'd like to pay!

choices.feedback: 结账 (jiézhàng) works everywhere.
Not before paying! Call the server over first.

line.zh: 我看一下……一共{total}块，包括茶位费。
line.zht: 我看一下……一共{total}塊，包括茶位費。
line.py: Wǒ kàn yíxià… yígòng {total} kuài, bāokuò cháwèi fèi.
line.en: Let me see… ¥{total} in total, including the tea charge.

choices.feedback: Scan and done.
Cash is still accepted at most teahouses.
Good question to ask!

tea-fee.speaker: server

line.zh: 茶位费就是每个人的茶钱。
line.zht: 茶位費就是每個人的茶錢。
line.py: Cháwèi fèi jiù shì měi ge rén de chá qián.
line.en: The tea charge is just each person's tea money.

tea-fee.note: That's why your tea shows up on the bill ×2 — one for each of you.

line.zh: 谢谢，慢走！欢迎再来饮茶！
line.zht: 謝謝，慢走！歡迎再來飲茶！
line.py: Xièxie, màn zǒu! Huānyíng zài lái yǐnchá!
line.en: Thank you, take care! Come back for dim sum again!

bunStyle.note: Steamed buns are fluffy and white; baked ones have a sweet, golden glaze.

items.note: Earthy and dark — the most popular dim sum tea. Charged per person.
Chefs are judged by their 虾饺: thin, translucent skin and neat pleats.
Literally "phoenix claws" — a dim sum classic, braised in black bean sauce.
皮蛋 (century egg) is preserved for weeks — it's rich and savory, and much milder than it looks.
